enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable (single-wave cross-sectional design; however, cross-sectional sample loss is substantial, dropping from all Minas Gerais municipalities to 574 after undocumented boxplot outlier removal and to N = 391 in the final regressions due to missing SNIS/IBGE values).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: although the literature review and bivariate chi-square/ANOVA analyses recognize strong differences by municipal population size (porte populacional), socioeconomic development, and provider scale, the multiple linear regressions include only the four institutional capacity factor scores with zero controls for population size, urbanization, income/HDI, region, or provider type, and suffer from cross-sectional simultaneity/reverse causality (e.g., operational revenues/expenditures depend on existing service coverage, and low-water-access municipalities adopt plans reactively).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-adequate: legal-institutional instruments under Federal Law No. 11.445/2007 are operationalized solely as two binary (1/0) self-reported SNIS indicators for the existence of a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (PMSB, N = 456) and Municipal Public Sanitation Policy (PPSB, N = 471) in 2018, without assessing statutory compliance, plan quality, enforcement, or service-provider contract type, and with substantial municipal non-reporting.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: both exposure and outcome variables rely on self-reported SNIS municipal/provider records (2018) and asynchronous IBGE municipal staffing records (2017); as the authors acknowledge, data reporting into SNIS is itself correlated with the service provider's institutional capacity, introducing differential measurement error.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate concern: access to water supply (Atend_Agua), sanitary sewerage (Atend_Esgoto), and household solid waste collection (Atend_RDO) use standardized SNIS percentage indicators, but rely on unverified provider self-declarations, condition sewerage coverage on municipalities served with water, and measure nominal coverage rather than water quality, continuity, or sewage treatment.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: no pre-analysis plan or protocol is reported, and baseline municipality counts, specific boxplot outlier thresholds, and sensitivity analyses for excluded cases are omitted; however, all three hypothesized outcome models—including counter-hypothesized negative and statistically null political-capacity coefficients—are transparently reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: starting from the municipalities of Minas Gerais, an unspecified number of observations were removed as outliers via boxplots (leaving N = 574 for most variables) and listwise deletion of missing data (particularly non-reported PMSB and PPSB) further restricted the regression sample to N = 391, excluding more than half of the state's municipalities and likely underrepresenting smaller, lower-capacity municipalities that fail to report to SNIS.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 3.1 defines the target universe as municipalities of Minas Gerais using 2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE data, but never reports the initial number of municipalities retrieved, the specific quantitative thresholds used to delete 'a large number of outliers' via boxplots (leaving N = 574), or criteria governing listwise exclusion down to N = 391 in the regressions.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 16-17 / pp. 447-448); Section 4, Table 2 & text (PDF pp. 19, 22 / pp. 450, 453)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The setting (municipalities of Minas Gerais, Brazil in 2017-2018), regional distribution of municipal plans/policies (Figure 2, highlighting RMBH, Vale do Rio Doce and Zona da Mata), population size tiers in bivariate analyses, and full descriptive statistics (mean, SD, min, max, skewness, kurtosis in Table 2) are clearly described.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF p. 10 / p. 441); Section 3.1 (PDF pp. 16-18 / pp. 447-449); Section 4, Table 2 & Figure 2 (PDF pp. 19-21 / pp. 450-452)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Institutional capacity was operationalized through 10 indicators from SNIS (2018) and IBGE (2017) grouped via PCA/varimax into 4 factors (KMO = 0.675, 78.51% variance explained). Reliability and construct validity are uncertain because SNIS inputs are self-declared by providers (correlating reporting quality with institutional capacity), technical-staffing variables come from 2017 while other variables are from 2018, and PMSB/PPSB are binary (1/0) presence indicators that do not capture plan quality or implementation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1, Table 1 (PDF pp. 17-18 / pp. 448-449); Section 4, Table 3 (PDF pp. 20, 22 / pp. 451, 453); Section 5 (PDF p. 26 / p. 457)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: All municipal sanitation and institutional indicators were drawn from standardized national administrative definitions maintained by SNIS and IBGE and statutory requirements under Federal Law No. 11.445/2007 applied uniformly across municipalities.

In the literature review and exploratory bivariate tests (Chi-square and ANOVA), the authors note that municipal population size (porte populacional), population density, socioeconomic/HDI disparities, geographic location, and service-provider scale strongly covary with both municipal institutional capacity and sanitation coverage, but they do not formally identify these structural variables as confounders for the regression specification.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 13-14 / pp. 444-445); Section 3.1 (PDF p. 16 / p. 447); Section 4 (PDF pp. 21, 24 / pp. 452, 455)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No confounding-control strategy was stated or implemented in the multivariable regressions. Table 4 includes only the four institutional capacity factor scores as predictors, omitting municipal population size, urbanization, GDP per capita/HDI, regional fixed effects, and provider type (municipal vs. state utility/private), leaving severe omitted-variable bias and reverse causality unaddressed.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 18-19 / pp. 449-450); Section 4, Table 4 (PDF pp. 22-23 / pp. 453-454)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes (Atend_Agua, Atend_Esgoto, Atend_RDO) come from official SNIS 2018 indicators, but Section 5 explicitly notes that SNIS data are self-declared by service providers and that feeding data into SNIS may itself depend on provider institutional capacity; furthermore, Atend_Esgoto is conditioned on municipalities served with water and measures connection coverage rather than wastewater treatment.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1, Table 1 (PDF p. 17 / p. 448); Section 4, Table 2 (PDF p. 19 / p. 450); Section 5 (PDF p. 26 / p. 457)

domain_ratings.justification: Although VIF, Shapiro-Wilk, and White's heteroskedasticity test with robust standard errors were applied, the statistical workflow has major flaws: (1) dichotomous variables (PMSB, PPSB, Tecnico_Agua, Tecnico_Esgoto) were entered into Pearson-correlation PCA rather than tetrachoric/polychoric factor analysis; (2) undocumented boxplot outlier removal and listwise deletion eliminated over half of Minas Gerais's municipalities (final N = 391); (3) bounded percentage outcomes (0-100%) were modeled by unadjusted OLS with zero demographic/socioeconomic controls; and (4) strong simultaneity/endogeneity exists between per-capita sanitation revenues/expenditures/staffing, reactive plan adoption, and coverage rates.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.2 (PDF pp. 18-19 / pp. 449-450); Section 4, Tables 2-4 (PDF pp. 19, 22-23 / pp. 450, 453-454)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This analytical cross-sectional study examines the association between municipal institutional capacity (financial, technical, operational and political factor scores derived from 2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE indicators) and water, sewerage and solid-waste coverage across municipalities in Minas Gerais, Brazil. Appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies, the study raises High concern for risk of bias (2 Yes, 4 Unclear, 2 No). Key threats to internal and external validity include: (1) severe selection and missing-data bias, as undocumented boxplot outlier removal reduced the sample to 574 municipalities and missing SNIS/IBGE data (especially non-reported municipal sanitation plans and policies) further restricted the regression sample to N = 391; (2) unadjusted confounding and simultaneity/reverse causality, as the OLS regressions omit all structural municipal confounders (such as population size, urbanization, income/HDI and service-provider type) while using endogenous per-capita sanitation revenues/expenditures and reactive plan adoption to predict contemporaneous coverage; (3) use of Pearson-correlation PCA on binary legal/technical indicators; and (4) self-reported SNIS administrative measurements whose completeness and accuracy depend on municipal institutional capacity itself.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Quantitative analytical cross-sectional observational study (municipal-level principal-components factor analysis and OLS multiple linear regression with robust standard errors)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF pp. 6-7 / pp. 437-438); Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 7-10 / pp. 438-441); Section 2.2 Literature Review (PDF pp. 12-16 / pp. 443-447); Section 3 Methodological Procedures, Table 1 (PDF pp. 16-19 / pp. 447-450); Section 4 Results and Discussion, Tables 2-4 & Figure 2 (PDF pp. 19-25 / pp. 450-456); Section 5 Final Considerations (PDF pp. 25-26 / pp. 456-457).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes single-period cross-sectional observational municipal data (2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE) using exploratory factor analysis and multiple linear regression across municipalities in Minas Gerais, without randomization, longitudinal follow-up, or a quasi-experimental policy/intervention comparator structure; therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
